\title{Can Referees Rely on Automated Reference Checks?\\Diagnosing and Reducing False Alarms in CheckIfExist}

\author{
    Diletta Abbonato\textsuperscript{1,*} \\
    \small \textsuperscript{1}CPS Department, University of Turin, Turin, Italy \\
    \small \textsuperscript{*}Corresponding author: \texttt{diletta.abbonato@unito.it}
}
\date{}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent Automated reference checks are entering peer review, and referees are increasingly expected to run them. Such a tool helps only if it surfaces wrong references without burying them among correct ones. An independent evaluation found that the most sensitive tools flag about half of the genuine references in a verified test set. This paper takes one of them, CheckIfExist, and asks where its false alarms come from and whether they can be removed without loss of detection. A diagnosis combining the source code with \Nrefs{} reference strings from \Npapers{} papers traces the errors to properties of citation practice, PDF extraction and bibliographic indexing that vary across fields. On the independent test set, whose published result we first reproduce, the revised tool detects \IndRevTP{} of \IndProb{} problematic references and flags \IndRevFP{} of \IndGen{} genuine ones, against \IndBaseTP{} and \IndBaseFP{} for the original. On altered references constructed after the revision was fixed, detection rises from \ConDetBase{}\% to \ConDetRev{}\% while false alarms remain low. On references extracted from real manuscripts, fabrications hidden among them in the manuscripts' own style are flagged in \PlantDetRev{}\% of cases rather than \PlantDetBase{}\%. Regressions on these references show that the revision removes false alarms caused by extraction and web pages, but not those caused by styles that omit titles. We would maintain that the binding constraint on automated reference checking is not detection but restraint, and that much of what limits restraint lies in the scholarly record rather than in any particular tool.

\vspace{6pt}
\noindent \textbf{Keywords:} Peer review; Reference verification; Citation accuracy; Research integrity; Bibliographic databases; Large language models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Reference verification has moved into the editorial workflow. Language models fabricate bibliographic references under a wide range of conditions \citep{bhattacharyya2023, walters2023, day2023}, and a series of recent audits documents such references in the published record itself, in conference proceedings and on preprint servers alike \citep{sakai2026, zhao2026, russinovich2026, naturesocsci2026, naturepolluting2026}. Publishers now screen submissions, arXiv suspends authors who submit unchecked machine-generated references \citep{naturebanned2026}, and referees are increasingly expected to check the bibliographies of the manuscripts they review. A number of tools have appeared to help them, ranging from open scripts to services combining database retrieval with language models \citep{abbonato2026, russinovich2026, shi2026, khajavi2026}.

What a referee needs from such a tool can be stated simply. It should surface the references that are wrong, and it should not bury them among references that are correct. The two requirements pull in opposite directions, since every rule that makes a checker more suspicious also makes it suspicious of more genuine references, and a referee confronted with many flags per manuscript will reasonably stop reading them. The literature on citation verification has concentrated on the first requirement. Evaluations report how many fabricated references a system detects, typically on benchmarks in which fabrications are generated for the purpose, and it is generally acknowledged that performance on references observed in the wild is lower \citep{shi2026}. The second requirement has received much less attention, and yet it is the one that determines whether a tool is usable in peer review at all.

Independent evidence suggests that it is also the binding one. \citet{badalova2026} compared five verification tools on references from three scholarly documents, each manually checked against publisher and repository records. The tools that detected nearly all problematic references also flagged a large share of genuine ones, and the authors conclude that none was reliable enough to support a decision without manual verification. They attribute the difficulty to reference extraction errors, incomplete metadata, limited database coverage and inconsistent verification results. The present paper takes one of the tools they evaluated, CheckIfExist, of which the author is the developer \citep{abbonato2026}, and asks three questions. Where do its false alarms come from? Can they be removed without loss of detection? And what, as a result, does a referee see when checking the bibliography of a manuscript?

The answers are sought in three steps. The first is a diagnosis that combines a reading of the source code with a large corpus of reference strings extracted from the bibliographies of preprints and conference papers, audited for this study. The second is a revision of the tool addressing each cause identified, fixed before evaluation. The third is an evaluation on the independent test set of \citet{badalova2026}, where the published result is first reproduced, on a set of altered references constructed after the revision was fixed, and on reference strings extracted from real manuscripts, among which fabricated references written in the same style were then hidden. The comparison with RefChecker \citep{russinovich2026}, which the same independent study evaluated, provides an external benchmark.

The exercise is of interest beyond the tool. The causes identified turn out to be properties of citation practice and of the bibliographic infrastructure rather than of the software: the division of DOI registration between agencies that are queried separately, citation styles that omit titles and are concentrated in particular fields, the text layer of compiled PDFs, to which reference parsers are known to be sensitive \citep{lopez2009, tkaczyk2015}, and the incompleteness of author lists in open metadata. They will therefore affect every checker built on the same open sources, and any bibliometric study that relies on such checks to estimate the prevalence of fabricated or erroneous citations.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section~\ref{sec:data} describes the tool, its revision and the evaluation design. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports where the errors come from, how the revised tool performs, and what a referee sees. Section~\ref{sec:disc} discusses the implications and the limitations of the evidence.

\section{Data and methods}
\label{sec:data}

\subsection{The instrument and its revision}
\label{sec:tool}

CheckIfExist is an open-source web application, running entirely in the browser, that verifies bibliographic references against five open sources: Crossref, OpenAlex \citep{priem2022}, Semantic Scholar, arXiv and DBLP \citep{abbonato2026}. It is deterministic, in the sense that it uses no language model and applies explicit rules to the records it retrieves, and only reference strings leave the user's machine, never the manuscript itself. A reference can be checked individually, as part of a pasted bibliography, from a BibTeX file, or from a PDF whose bibliography the tool extracts. In each case the original tool shows the result with one of four labels: \emph{Verified} when the match confidence exceeds 80, \emph{Partial Match} above 50, \emph{Mismatch} below, and \emph{Not Found} when no source returns a sufficiently similar record. The revised tool adds two labels for entries it cannot check as references, \emph{Extraction problem} and \emph{Web resource}, described below. We treat any label other than Verified as a flag, that is, as a reference the referee must inspect, which is also the definition used by \citet{badalova2026}.

The revision addressed each cause of error identified in the diagnosis of Section~\ref{sec:diagnosis}, and Table~\ref{tab:revision} lists them. The causes fall into two groups. The first concerns references that were accepted when they should not have been, and the corresponding checks can only lower the confidence of a match, never raise it. The second concerns genuine references that were flagged, and here the revisions either find the record by other means or report the reason a reference cannot be checked, instead of reporting it as not found.

The revision was fixed in the public repository before any evaluation began. Corrections were made afterwards on four occasions, each prompted by defects that an evaluation brought to light, and all are recorded in the public history of the code. The year check read a year out of arXiv identifiers, which came to light on the independent test set. The detection of title text depended on letter case, so that a title cited in title case was taken for a missing one, which came to light while measuring the prevalence of title-less references in the diagnostic corpus. The path that verifies references by volume and page did not apply the title check, which came to light on the constructed set. And the new comparisons mishandled text in the form PDF extraction delivers it and names in the form sources record them, with words broken across lines, accents separated from their letters, compound surnames and given names reduced to initials, while the choice among the records a search returns could prefer a record whose title merely contains the cited one; these came to light on the manuscripts. Where a correction followed the evaluation of a set, the results of the version evaluated blind on that set are reported alongside those of the final version.

\subsection{Evaluation design}
\label{sec:design}

Five sets of references are used, for different purposes. The \emph{diagnostic corpus} consists of \Nrefs{} reference strings extracted from the bibliographies of \Npapers{} arXiv preprints and NeurIPS proceedings papers spanning 2016 to 2026, in nine venue-year strata, and serves to measure how often the features associated with errors occur. It was audited for this study: every string left unresolved by a single-source check, and a stratified random sample of the strings it accepted, were resolved individually, and the identifier or URL supporting each verdict is released with the data.

The \emph{independent test set} is that of \citet{badalova2026data}: \IndN{} references from \IndDocs{} documents, of which \IndProb{} were judged problematic by manual verification and \IndGen{} genuine, released with the outputs of the five tools. The public file was saved in an encoding that cannot represent typographic quotes, dashes or some Central European letters, and \IndRestoredChars{} characters in \IndRestoredRefs{} references had been replaced by question marks. They were restored by rules that follow from the citation styles of the three documents, and every substitution is logged.

The \emph{constructed set} was built after the revision was fixed, from \ConGen{} references of the diagnostic corpus whose Crossref record matched on title and year, re-fetched by DOI and formatted in APA style. Each yields a genuine reference and an altered one, \ConKindN{} of each of four kinds: an \emph{invented} work, keeping the first author but splicing the title with that of another reference from the same stratum; an \emph{extended} title, in which a real title is followed by invented words; \emph{swapped} authors, in which a real title carries the authors of another paper; and \emph{altered} metadata, in which title and authors are correct but year and venue are not. The first three are fabrications, the fourth a citation error of the kind a referee should still notice. Half of the pairs carry the real DOI in both versions, since fabricated references often carry real identifiers.

The \emph{manuscripts} are the reference strings of \CorpMss{} papers of the diagnostic corpus, three per stratum, \CorpRefs{} in all, as the corpus pipeline extracted them from the PDFs. They are what a referee would submit to the tool, with the damage that extraction does to them, but they are not always complete bibliographies: the pipeline kept at most the first fifty strings of each paper, and for \CorpFew{} of the \CorpMss{} papers it recovered five or fewer. Results on them are therefore reported per fifty references rather than per paper.

The \emph{planted set} supplies what the manuscripts lack, fabricated references in the form in which a referee would meet them. Neither version of the tool was run on it before the final version was fixed. It was built by editing reference strings of the same manuscripts that both versions of the tool had verified: \PlantN{} fabrications of the three kinds defined above, between \PlantKindMin{} and \PlantKindMax{} of each kind, from \PlantMss{} manuscripts. Each keeps the citation style, the extraction damage and any identifier of the string it was made from, and the donor of the second half of an invented title, of the words added to an extended one or of a swapped author list is another reference of the same bibliography.

The tool was run outside the browser on the same code path as the web interface, with three differences that do not touch its logic. A standard XML parser replaces the browser's; requests that the tool routes to arXiv through a public proxy, needed in the browser for cross-origin reasons, go to arXiv directly; and requests are paced at the rates the sources ask for, with retries on transient errors except to Semantic Scholar, which the tool itself does not retry. Every response, failures included, was stored, so that the original and the revised tool saw identical responses to identical requests and differences between them measure the tool rather than the network. Three of the five sources contributed little or nothing. DBLP answered each of the \DBLPRequests{} requests made to it with a page asking the client to prove that it was not a robot, instead of data. Of the \STwoRequests{} requests made to Semantic Scholar's unauthenticated service, \STwoAnswered{}\% received an answer, and none of these contained a paper; \STwoRejected{} were rejected because both versions of the tool ask for a field that the service no longer supports, and the rest went unanswered. OpenAlex, whose free tier at the time allowed about a hundred searches before its allowance was exhausted, answered \OAAnswered{}\% of \OARequests{}. Crossref and arXiv answered \CRAnswered{}\% and \AXAnswered{}\%. The results therefore describe a tool working almost entirely from Crossref and arXiv, with occasional help from OpenAlex. The condition affects the original and the revised tool alike, and it may well be that of a referee using the tool without API keys, but absolute rates obtained with all five sources available would differ from those reported here.

RefChecker \citep{russinovich2026} provides the external comparison. On the independent set we use the results published by \citet{badalova2026}, obtained in its default configuration. On the constructed set we ran version 3.0.190 ourselves, without a language model. In that configuration it cannot segment a plain-text bibliography, so both tools were given the same BibTeX file, which CheckIfExist processes through its own BibTeX path.

The two versions of CheckIfExist are always compared on the same references, and differences in the share of references flagged are tested with exact McNemar tests on the references whose verdict changes. On the manuscripts, whose references are clustered within papers, two further estimates are made with linear probability models, with standard errors clustered by manuscript. The first is the change in the share of references presented as possibly wrong, with reference fixed effects on the two versions stacked. The second is the association between that outcome and the features of reference strings measured in the diagnosis, with stratum fixed effects, estimated separately for each version. A linear model is used because, under the revised tool, some features predict the outcome perfectly, which rules out a logit.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Where the errors come from}
\label{sec:diagnosis}

The audit of the diagnostic corpus provides the starting point. A single-source check of the kind commonly deployed, submitting each string to Crossref and accepting the first record returned, leaves \Nflag{} strings unresolved, and individual resolution found no fabricated reference among them: the flags consisted of segmentation failures, text that is not a reference, references the rule could not match, and works no source indexes. The same check is, if anything, more worrying in the other direction, since only \Pcmatchcorrect{}\% of the references it accepts correspond to the work cited and \Pcmatchwrong{}\% resolve to a different publication. A permissive check thus produces false alarms and false reassurance at once, and a referee has no way of telling which is which.

The source code of CheckIfExist shows how the same two failures arise in a tool that queries several sources and compares what it retrieves. The misses have a common origin in acceptance rules that ask whether a record is compatible with the citation rather than whether it is the work cited: containment of a title, trust in an identifier, and a year disagreement that was computed and then discarded. The false alarms have more varied origins, and most of them are properties of the references and of the indexes rather than of the software. Table~\ref{tab:features} reports how often the corresponding features occur in the diagnostic corpus.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Features of reference strings associated with errors of automated checking, as a percentage of strings in each stratum of the diagnostic corpus. Title-less references are single references with no stretch of four or more words between punctuation marks; merged entries contain several references run together.}
\label{tab:features}
\vspace{4pt}
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\input{table_features}
\end{table}

Three patterns stand out. The first is the dependence on field. References that carry no title, the norm in the styles of physics and astronomy, are \FeatNoTitleGen{}\% of the strings in the general 2026 cohort, where those fields are represented, against \FeatNoTitleNipsTwentythree{}\% in NeurIPS 2023; a checker that matches on titles fails on them systematically, and fails more often in some fields than in others. The second is the dependence on time, which runs in both directions. Ligature glyphs in the extracted text, which the original normalization deleted, occur in \FeatLigCsSixteen{}\% of the arXiv \textit{cs.AI} strings of 2016 and in almost none of 2026, while arXiv identifiers, which route verification through a path that did not compare authors, grow from \FeatArxivCsSixteen{}\% to \FeatArxivCsTwentyfive{}\% of \textit{cs.AI} references between 2016 and 2025. The third is the weight of extraction itself. Entries that are not references at all reach \FeatNotRefNipsTwentyfive{}\% of the NeurIPS 2025 strings, and merged entries are most frequent, at \FeatMergedGen{}\%, in the cohort that includes astronomy bibliographies, whose unnumbered styles give a PDF segmenter nothing to split on.

\subsection{How the revised tool performs}
\label{sec:performance}

Table~\ref{tab:independent} reports the results on the independent test set. The first step is replication. Run through the single-reference path, which appears to be the one the independent study used, the original tool reproduces the published confusion matrix within two cases in each cell. Agreement reference by reference is lower, at \IndAgreeQuick{}\%, and through the pasted-bibliography path it is \IndAgreePaste{}\%. Of the \IndDisQuick{} references classified differently on the single-reference path, \IndDisQuickGen{} are genuine, and the differences are consistent with the fluctuating availability of sources at different times, which decides whether a genuine reference is found at all.

The revised tool detects \IndRevTP{} of the \IndProb{} problematic references, against \IndBaseTP{} for the original, and flags \IndRevFP{} of the \IndGen{} genuine ones, against \IndBaseFP{}: false alarms fall by \IndFPDrop{}\% while detection does not decline. The fall is well beyond chance: every one of the \TestIndFARLost{} genuine references whose verdict changes passes from flagged to verified (exact McNemar test, \TestIndFARP{}), and the share of genuine references flagged goes from \IndBaseFAR{}\% (95\% interval \TestIndFARBaseLo{} to \TestIndFARBaseHi{}) to \IndRevFAR{}\% (\TestIndFARRevLo{} to \TestIndFARRevHi{}). The gain in detection, \TestIndDetGained{} references, is within chance (\TestIndDetP{}). RefChecker, in the published evaluation, detects \IndRCTP{} problematic references and flags \IndRCFP{} genuine ones. Figure~\ref{fig:independent} places the two versions of CheckIfExist among the five tools evaluated by the independent study. Before the revision, the tools that detect most problematic references, CheckIfExist included, also flag the most genuine ones, so that greater detection is bought with more false alarms; the revised tool moves off that frontier rather than along it.

Some qualification is needed before reading these figures as a comparison between tools. The independent set is small, the published RefChecker results were obtained at another time and through another interface, and a few of its cases were inspected during the diagnosis, before the revision was written. The set was not used to tune the revision, and the version frozen before evaluation flags \IndFrozenFP{} genuine references rather than \IndRevFP{}, the difference being due to two of the corrections described in Section~\ref{sec:tool}, to the year check and to the choice among the records a search returns. Nonetheless it cannot be treated as fully held out, and the constructed set exists for that reason.

Table~\ref{tab:constructed} reports the results on the constructed set, which was built after the revision was fixed and is therefore the cleaner test. Both versions flag almost none of the genuine references, which are formatted from their own Crossref records and pose none of the difficulties of references extracted from PDFs: \ConFARBase{}\% for the original tool and \ConFARRev{}\% for the revised one. Both also flag every invented work. The difference lies in the three kinds in which a real work is cited wrongly. The original tool accepted most extended titles and about half of the references with swapped authors or altered metadata, and it did so above all when the citation carried the work's real DOI: it flagged \ConDetBaseDOI{}\% of the altered references with a DOI, against \ConDetBaseNoDOI{}\% of those without. The revised tool flags \ConDetRev{}\% of all altered references, against \ConDetBase{}\%, and \ConDetRevDOI{}\% of those carrying a DOI. The rise in detection involves \TestConDetGained{} references and is well beyond chance (\TestConDetP{}); the fall in false alarms, which were rare to begin with, involves \TestConFARLost{} references and is within chance (\TestConFARP{}).

The altered references the revised tool still accepts fall into three groups, each traceable to a choice made in the revision. Extended titles are missed when the added words are few, or when they resemble words that legitimately follow a title in a reference, such as \emph{tutorial}, \emph{review} or \emph{press}, which the check disregards. Swapped authors are missed when the citation names a single author, since the check requires two names absent from the record so as not to react to a stray token. And one altered year falls within the tolerance allowed for preprint records. The evaluation also revealed a defect: the path that verifies references by volume and page did not apply the title check, and let one extended title through. It was corrected afterwards. The final version, which also includes the corrections prompted by the manuscripts, differs from the version evaluated blind in \ConFinalChanged{} references of this set: it flags that extended title, and it verifies a genuine reference whose record title, as Crossref returns it, is broken across lines by markup. It detects \ConDetRevFinal{}\% of the altered references and flags \ConFARRevFinal{}\% of the genuine ones.

RefChecker, given the same references in BibTeX, shows the trade-off between the two requirements in another form. Counting its warnings, as the independent study did, it detects \ConDetRC{}\% of the altered references but flags \ConFARRC{}\% of the genuine ones; for \RCGenYearVenue{} of the \RCGenFlagged{} genuine references it flags, the only objection is a warning on the year, almost always a difference of one year, or on the form of the venue's name. Counting errors only, it flags \ConFARRCStrict{}\% of the genuine references but detects \ConDetRCStrict{}\% of the altered ones, missing most extended titles and nearly all altered metadata. Given the same BibTeX, the final version of CheckIfExist flags \ConFARRevBib{}\% of the genuine references and detects \ConDetRevBib{}\% of the altered ones, against \ConFARBaseBib{}\% and \ConDetBaseBib{}\% for the original, and so does better on both counts than RefChecker in either configuration. The structured fields of BibTeX make author lists and years easier to compare, and the original tool already detects every swapped author list and every altered year there; what it misses are extended titles, \ConDetBaseBibExtended{}\% of which it flags against \ConDetRevBibExtended{}\% for the final version. The comparison should be read with one caveat: RefChecker was run without the language model it uses, in its default configuration, to extract references from text and to assess suspected fabrications.

\subsection{What a referee sees}
\label{sec:referee}

The unit a referee works with is the manuscript, not the reference, and the relevant question is how many references the tool asks them to inspect and what those references turn out to be. Figure~\ref{fig:referee}(a) gives the answer for the manuscripts, per fifty references.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_referee.pdf}
\caption{What a referee sees. (a) References flagged per fifty in the reference strings of the \CorpMss{} manuscripts, by the label the tool shows: not found, partial match or mismatch, which present a reference as possibly wrong, and extraction problem or web resource, which report that it could not be checked. (b) Share of the \PlantN{} fabrications hidden in the same manuscripts that each version flags, by kind.}
\label{fig:referee}
\end{figure}

The original tool flags \CorpFlagFiftyBase{} references in every fifty, and it presents all of them in the same way, as references not found or not matching their record, that is, as references that may be wrong. The version of the revision evaluated blind flags \CorpFlagFiftyRevBlind{}, but what the flags say is different. Only \CorpScrutFiftyRevBlind{} in fifty present a reference as possibly wrong; the other \CorpLimitFiftyRevBlind{} report that the entry could not be checked, because extraction has not produced a single reference or because it cites a web page, which no bibliographic source indexes and which the referee can check by following the link.

With only \CorpMss{} manuscripts, these differences are estimated with some uncertainty. The change in the share of references presented as possibly wrong is \CorpDiffRevBlind{} percentage points in the version evaluated blind, with a 95\% interval from \CorpDiffRevBlindLo{} to \CorpDiffRevBlindHi{} that does not exclude no change (\CorpDiffRevBlindP{}), and \CorpDiffRev{} points in the final version (\CorpDiffRevLo{} to \CorpDiffRevHi{}, \CorpDiffRevP{}), whose corrections, however, were prompted by these same manuscripts.

Which references produce the flags is shown in Table~\ref{tab:regression}, which relates the probability that a string is presented as possibly wrong to the features measured in the diagnosis. Under the original tool, and within each stratum, a string without a title is \RegBaseNoTitle{} percentage points more likely to be presented as possibly wrong than an otherwise similar string, an entry that is not a reference \RegBaseNotRef{} points more likely, and one that cites a web page \RegBaseWeb{} points more likely; a word broken across lines adds \RegBaseHyphen{} points, while an arXiv identifier, which lets the record be resolved directly, lowers the probability by \RegBaseArxivAbs{} points. The revision removes the effect of merged entries, of entries that are not references and of web pages, which it reports as limits of the check rather than as suspicions (\RegChangeRevMergedP{}, \RegChangeRevNotRefP{} and \RegChangeRevWebP{} for the three changes). The effect of words broken across lines survives in the version evaluated blind, at \RegRevBlindHyphen{} points, and disappears with the correction, at \RegRevHyphen{} points (\RegChangeRevHyphenP{} for the change). What the revision does not remove is the effect of the missing title, \RegRevNoTitle{} points in the final version, a change of \RegChangeRevNoTitle{} points from the original that is not statistically significant (\RegChangeRevNoTitleP{}). Verification by first author, volume, page and year recovers some title-less references, but \RegRevNoTitleRate{}\% of them are still presented as possibly wrong, and the styles that omit titles remain the feature most strongly associated with false alarms.

Why the total did not fall is shown by the references that the original tool verified and the revision flagged. There were \CorpNewFlagsBlind{}, and \CorpNewFlagsBlindCleared{} of them came from defects in the revision itself, which the manuscripts brought to light: the handling of words broken across lines, which occur in \FeatHyphenAll{}\% of the strings of the diagnostic corpus, of accents separated from their letters, which occur in \FeatAccentAll{}\%, and of names in their various forms, and the choice among the records a search returns. The corrected version verifies them. Of the \ChangesN{} references that the final version still flags although the original tool verified them, each examined individually against the records the two versions selected, \ChangesOther{} had been verified by the original tool against a record of another work, such as a book review of 2001 for an article of 2011 on the same subject, and \ChangesVersion{} against another version of the work cited, a first edition for the third or an arXiv version whose title has since changed. These flags are the counterpart of the false reassurance described in Section~\ref{sec:diagnosis}: the original tool accepted such records, and the revised tool, unable to find the work cited among the sources it could reach, reports the disagreement instead. Of the rest, \ChangesDamage{} are entries in which extraction has run two references together, and in \ChangesLost{} the final version no longer retrieves a record that the original tool had found, because the cleaned text changes what a search returns or which segment the tool takes for the title. With the corrections, the final version flags \CorpFlagFiftyRev{} references in fifty, of which \CorpScrutFiftyRev{} as possibly wrong, \CorpScrutDropRev{}\% fewer than the original tool; on this set, however, it is not evaluated blind. The fall also has a cost. Of the \ClearedN{} references that the original tool flagged and the final version verifies, \ClearedRight{} are verified against the work cited, but \ClearedWrong{} against a record of another work: a fragment of text naming an organisation is taken for a chapter of the same title, and a paper is matched to a preprint whose title contains the cited one. Neither record lists authors, so that the author check has nothing to compare, and both were selected because of the last correction, which prefers the record whose title is the cited one and whose year agrees with the citation. Corrections made on the evidence of a set can thus introduce errors on that same set, a further reason to report the version evaluated blind.

What the flags that remain point to was established by verifying individually a random sample of \SampleN{} of the \CorpScrutNRev{} references that the final version presents as possibly wrong. Of these, \SampleCorrect{} are correct citations of works that exist. For \SampleCorrectNoCrossref{} of them Crossref has no record at all: they are papers in the proceedings of machine learning conferences, preprints, books, and articles in journals that Crossref does not cover, which only the sources that did not answer, or an arXiv search that did not return them, could have supplied. The other \SampleCorrectCrossref{} have a Crossref record, sometimes of another edition or version, which the tool's searches missed or matched imperfectly. Another \SampleDamage{} are strings that extraction has damaged: cut before the title, run together with another reference or with the running text, or garbled, as when the parentheses of a title in mathematical notation are read as letters. The sample also contains \SampleError{} genuine citation error, a word of a title replaced by another, and \SampleUnverifiable{} unpublished presentation at a project meeting that no source records. None of the references is fabricated. For a referee, then, the flags that remain on these manuscripts are almost all false alarms, and what produces them is less the rules of the tool than the reach of the sources it could query and the state of the text it was given.

Figure~\ref{fig:referee}(b) shows the other side of the ledger. The original tool flags \PlantDetBase{}\% of the fabrications hidden in the manuscripts and the final version \PlantDetRev{}\%, presenting \PlantDetScrutRev{}\% as possibly wrong and reporting the rest as extraction problems. The difference is well beyond chance, overall (\TestPlantP{}) and for each kind of fabrication taken separately (\TestPlantKindMaxP{} at most). By kind, the two versions flag \PlantDetBaseInvented{}\% and \PlantDetRevInvented{}\% of the invented works, \PlantDetBaseExtended{}\% and \PlantDetRevExtended{}\% of the extended titles, and \PlantDetBaseSwapped{}\% and \PlantDetRevSwapped{}\% of the swapped author lists. Extended titles written in the style of the manuscript are accepted by the original tool almost without exception, and they account for most of the difference. The fabrications the final version still accepts are, again, extended titles whose added words are too few to count, author lists that share a name with the record or that the record cannot contradict because it lists no authors, and a title that keeps only a few words of the real one. Put together, the two figures describe how much of a referee's attention the check directs to a fabrication. In a bibliography of fifty references of which one is fabricated, the original tool would present the fabrication, when it flags it, among \PlantNoiseBase{} other references presented as possibly wrong, and the final version among \PlantNoiseRev{}; the fabrication would account for \PlantShareBase{}\% of such flags in the first case and \PlantShareRev{}\% in the second. The revision thus makes a fabrication both more likely to be flagged and less likely to be lost among the flags. It does not make the list short: a referee who follows every flag that presents a reference as possibly wrong would still examine, on average, \PlantNoiseRev{} other references for each fabrication found, most of them correct.

\section{Discussion and conclusions}
\label{sec:disc}

This paper has asked whether a referee can rely on an automated reference check, taking one open tool as the object of study. The evidence suggests that the answer depends less on the tool's ability to find problematic references, which was already high, than on its ability to leave correct references alone, and that the second can be improved substantially once the causes of false alarms are identified. On the independent test set the revision reduces false alarms by \IndFPDrop{}\% without loss of detection. On altered references constructed after it was fixed, it detects \ConDetRev{}\% rather than \ConDetBase{}\% without flagging more genuine references. On the references of real manuscripts it flags \PlantDetRev{}\% of the fabrications hidden among them rather than \PlantDetBase{}\%, while presenting fewer genuine references as possibly wrong, by a margin that \CorpMss{} manuscripts measure only imprecisely before the corrections they prompted.

For referees, the practical implication concerns how a flag should be read. A flag from a verification tool is not a finding but an instruction to look, and its value lies in how much looking it saves. The revised tool distinguishes flags that call for scrutiny of the citation, such as a title that extends the record's, authors the record does not list, or a year that disagrees, from flags that describe the limits of the check, such as an extraction problem or a web page that no bibliographic database indexes. The second kind still requires a glance, but not suspicion. It seems likely that the credibility of automated checking in peer review will depend on this distinction as much as on the aggregate rates.

For those building such tools, four lessons seem to generalise. The first is that acceptance rules should test identity rather than compatibility: a record whose title is contained in the citation, whose identifier appears in it, or which lists no authors that could contradict the cited ones, is compatible with the citation without being the work cited, and the most common fabrications exploit precisely that gap. The second is that a resolved identifier is not evidence that a citation is correct, only that it points somewhere; the remainder of the citation has to agree with where it points. The third is that open bibliographic infrastructure is heterogeneous in ways that a checker must represent explicitly. DOIs are registered by more than one agency, author lists in open metadata are sometimes incomplete, some citation styles omit the title altogether, and free interfaces are rate limited, or closed to automated clients, to the point of unavailability. None of these is a defect of any single source, and none is visible in an evaluation that uses fabrications alone. The fourth is that a checker must be tested on references in the form in which extraction delivers them. The defects corrected last in this study, in the handling of words broken across lines and of accents separated from their letters, left no trace on references formatted from clean metadata. They appeared only on strings extracted from PDFs, where line-break hyphenation alone occurs in \FeatHyphenAll{}\% of the strings of the diagnostic corpus.

For bibliometric research, the results add to a well-documented literature on database coverage \citep{martinmartin2018, visser2021, verabaceta2019} a point specific to the verification of references. The error rates of a checker depend on the citation styles and extraction conditions of the literature it is applied to, and those vary across fields and over time, as Table~\ref{tab:features} shows. On the manuscripts, a reference in a style without titles is \RegBaseNoTitle{} percentage points more likely to be presented as possibly wrong than an otherwise similar one under the original tool, and \RegRevNoTitle{} points under the revised one (Table~\ref{tab:regression}). Estimates of the prevalence of fabricated citations that rely on automated checks, and comparisons of such estimates across fields or periods, therefore inherit a bias whose direction and size depend on the checker's rules. It would seem prudent for such studies to report the false-alarm behaviour of their checker on genuine references from the same fields, alongside its detection rate.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The independent test set is small and was assembled as a convenience sample, and a few of its cases were inspected during the diagnosis, so that it cannot be treated as fully held out. The constructed and planted sets were built after the tool was fixed, but their alterations are generated by rule, following the typology of fabrications reported in the literature \citep{russinovich2026, shi2026}, and fabrications produced by language models in the wild may differ from them. The corrections made after the revision was fixed were each prompted by an evaluation, so that on the set that prompted them the final version is not evaluated blind; this is why the results of the version evaluated blind are reported as well, and why the fabrications planted in the manuscripts were run only once the final version was fixed. Some weaknesses shared by both versions were left as they were, since changing them would have altered the tool beyond the causes diagnosed: the query sent to arXiv, which the service reads as a disjunction of words, and the heuristic that extracts a title from a reference string, which splits a title at its commas. The manuscripts are represented by the reference strings the corpus pipeline extracted, which for some papers are incomplete, so that the results on them are rates per reference rather than counts per paper; and they are few, so that differences between the versions on them are estimated with wide intervals. The corpus covers computer science, quantitative biology and one general cohort, in texts almost entirely in English, and the prevalence of the features in Table~\ref{tab:features} will differ elsewhere. The evaluation ran the tool outside the browser, with differences that do not touch its logic but do affect which sources were available when; Semantic Scholar and DBLP returned no data and OpenAlex did so only intermittently, so that the absolute rates describe a tool working almost entirely from Crossref and arXiv. The author developed the tool evaluated here; the use of an independently built and labelled test set, the reproduction of its published result, and the release of all code, data and outputs are intended to limit, not remove, the consequences of that position. Finally, no referee was observed using the tool. Whether the reduction in false alarms translates into time saved and errors caught in actual peer review is an empirical question that a study with referees would need to address, and it is the natural next step.

The conclusion we would draw is a cautious one. Automated reference checking can already detect most problematic references, and on the evidence reported here it can also be made considerably more restrained. What limits it is, to a large extent, not the software but the scholarly record it consults: the way references are extracted, the styles in which they are written, and the coverage and completeness of the open metadata against which they are checked. A referee can rely on such a tool to direct attention, and not to replace it.
